title: Hester's Harvest Tea Mix-Up
markdown:
The sun poked its head over Bramblewood Ridge, painting the sky pink and gold. Golden beams splashed across dew-kissed buttercups. Dawn broke. Today was THE day: the annual Harvest Tea. Hester the rabbit, nose twitching with anticipation, popped out of her cozy burrow.

Every day for Hester was about order. Neat rows of carrots, carefully stacked pebbles. Planning made her happy. For weeks she had worked on the Harvest Tea seating chart, a masterpiece of tiny neat squares and lists. "Right then," she chirped, unfurling the scroll. "All the most wonderful talkers together. That's the secret key to a splendid party!" She'd put Mrs. Higgins, the wren who knew every bit of gossip, right next to Eirwen Buttercup, the farmer with a laugh as big and booming as a drum. Professor Quill, the wise old owl who could spin tales, was right beside them. The plan was perfect. Or she thought it was.

Guests arrived, a parade of rustles and chirps. Tables piled with juicy berry tarts and honeyed nuts. Then a peculiar thing: all the most enthusiastic conversationalists bunched together. Mrs. Higgins told a thrilling squirrel-heist tale, Eirwen added booming sound effects, Professor Quill wove in a talking acorn. A cheerful thundercloud of chatter, all in one spot.

The other tables? Quiet. Penelope Pipkin, a shy field mouse, nibbled a berry. "Oh my," she whispered to a slow-moving beetle. "They do have a lot to say over there." The beetle blinked. Mayor Reed, a badger who usually bellowed greetings that made teacups dance, found himself stuck in a polite loop.

"After you, Mayor Reed," said Mrs. Pebble, a hedgehog with prickles like needles, pushing seed cakes.

"No, no, Mrs. Pebble, you should partake first." His voice lacked its happy bounce. "Your gardening tips are always so pertinent."

"Oh, thank you, Mayor. And your mayoral duties sound quite important."

It felt more like a quiet pond than a joyous party.

Down below, emerging from his tunnels, Sol the mole blinked in the bright light, paws dusty. Sol wasn't one for grand speeches, but he was good at noticing. He noticed the peculiar quiet. He noticed the knot of chatter, like a bird trapped in a corner.

Then he saw Mayor Reed, a little lost. Sol nudged Hester's paw. "Hester," he mumbled, voice like rolling pebbles. "The talking is all in one place. Like a jam jar with no air holes for the good ideas."

Hester's long ears drooped. She peered at the busy corner. Mrs. Higgins, Eirwen, and Professor Quill vibrating with excitement. Other tables hushed. Her perfect chart had worked too well. A politeness pile-up. A tremor through her whiskers. Not the joyous tea she had planned. A little bit sad.

She looked at the quiet faces. At Mayor Reed, who looked small. Her heart squeezed. A real mistake.

Mayor Reed caught her eye and gave a small polite nod. That was it. Hester's busy mind zapped. "Everyone! Please!" Small but clear, a bird's song. She hopped onto a moss-covered toadstool. The loud chatter paused. All eyes.

"I made a little mistake with the seating. I put all our best, most enthusiastic talkers in one spot. And it's not very good for everyone to have a good chat, is it?"

She didn't wait. "Come, come! Let's mix things up!" Quick paws, a quiet apology, guests shifting. She sat Eirwen Buttercup next to Penelope Pipkin, whose quiet observations would surely make him laugh. Mrs. Higgins near Sol, who had fascinating tales of underground earthworms. Mayor Reed at a table with Mrs. Pebble and Professor Quill, ideas sparking like tiny fireflies.

Suddenly the whole garden buzzed. Eirwen's hearty laugh boomed, and Penelope giggled, a sweet tinkling. Sol told a surprisingly funny story about a misplaced acorn; Mrs. Higgins listened with wide eyes. Mayor Reed and Mrs. Pebble discovered a shared passion for compost. Cheerful chatter, clinking teacups, contented hums. A proper bubbling party at last.

Hester watched, heart swelling with relief. The sun felt brighter. The tarts tasted sweeter. She did not declare the day amazing to the ridge. She joined the merry garden, hop-ready.

"I wonder," she said to Sol, "whether next year's chart should put one quiet mouse at every loud table on purpose — and whether Eirwen's laugh still fits on a tiny square."

Sol, who preferred tunnels to squares, thought it might, if you left air holes.
